title: Fine-tuning a language model: SFT, RLHF and when to bother
hook: Fine-tuning changes how a model behaves by default; most problems are solved more cheaply with a good prompt or RAG first.
inPlainWords: Fine-tuning continues training a model on your own examples so a behavior becomes its default, instead of something you have to ask for in every prompt. It's a bigger investment than prompting, worth it only for a clear, recurring gap.

useCase.title: The support bot's tone is close, but not quite ShopEase
useCase.story: Prompting gets the assistant most of the way, but it still occasionally writes overly formal apologies unlike ShopEase's brand voice, and misses house-style formatting for order summaries. Should the team fine-tune a model?

approaches.name: Prompting and RAG first
approaches.what: Fix behavior through instructions and retrieved context, with no training.
approaches.greatWhen: The behavior gap can be described in words and shown with a few examples in the prompt.
approaches.avoidWhen: The same correction has to be repeated in every prompt and still doesn't stick.
approaches.example: Adding brand-voice examples to the system prompt fixes most of the tone issue for free.

approaches.name: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT)
approaches.what: Continue training the model on examples of the exact input-output pairs you want, so the behavior becomes default.
approaches.greatWhen: The desired behavior is consistent, well-defined, and you have or can create enough quality examples.
approaches.avoidWhen: You have fewer than a few hundred good examples, or requirements change weekly.
approaches.example: A few thousand labeled order summaries in the house format.

approaches.name: Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) or preference tuning
approaches.what: Train the model to prefer outputs people rate higher, rather than matching one fixed example per input.
approaches.greatWhen: "Better versus worse" is easier for people to judge than to write out ahead of time, like tone and helpfulness.
approaches.avoidWhen: The team lacks a reliable way to compare outputs at scale, since noisy preferences train an unreliable model.
approaches.example: Raters compare two apology drafts and pick the better one, repeated thousands of times.

approaches.name: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (adapters)
approaches.what: Train a small add-on to the model instead of updating all its weights, far cheaper and faster.
approaches.greatWhen: You want the behavior change without the cost of full fine-tuning, or need multiple specialized variants.
approaches.avoidWhen: A full-weight fine-tune is required to change deep behavior.
approaches.example: A lightweight adapter for house style, swapped in only for order-summary tasks.

approaches.name: Don't fine-tune; wait for a better base model
approaches.what: Skip training, accept the current gap, and reassess as base models improve.
approaches.greatWhen: The gap is minor and new model releases keep narrowing it.
approaches.avoidWhen: The gap directly affects customer trust today.
approaches.example: The team notes the issue, checks it again after the next model upgrade, and skips training for now.

challenge.question: Prompting fixes most of the tone problem, but the formal-apology issue persists across many rewordings of the system prompt. What's the right next step?

options.text: Collect a few hundred to a few thousand examples of the corrected tone and run supervised fine-tuning
options.why: A consistent, well-defined behavior gap that prompting alone can't close is exactly what SFT is for, once enough examples exist.

options.text: Immediately run full RLHF with a new reward model
options.why: Could work, but RLHF needs comparison-based feedback and is heavier to set up; SFT with clear examples is the simpler first step for a well-defined gap.
The use case already shows this isn't converging.

options.text: Switch to a completely different base model
options.why: Untested, and doesn't address the specific, describable gap found.

bestCase.title: SFT closes a specific, well-defined gap
bestCase.example: The team collects 2,000 corrected apology and order-summary examples, fine-tunes, and the formal-tone issue drops from 1 in 5 responses to under 1 in 100, without needing brand-voice text in every prompt.

worstCase.title: Fine-tuning without enough examples
worstCase.example: The team fine-tunes on 40 examples. The model overfits to those exact phrasings, gets worse at handling questions slightly different from the examples, and nobody notices until complaints rise.

steps.label: Try prompting and RAG first
steps.goes: Brand-voice examples in the prompt fix most cases.
steps.goesWrong: The team skips straight to fine-tuning without trying the cheaper fix first.

steps.label: Measure what remains
steps.goes: 1 in 5 apologies is still too formal, consistently.

steps.label: Collect labeled examples
steps.goes: 2,000 corrected examples of the right tone.

steps.label: Run supervised fine-tuning
steps.goes: The model is retrained to default to the corrected tone.

steps.label: Test on held-out examples
steps.goes: The formal-tone rate drops to under 1 in 100.

steps.label: Watch for regressions elsewhere
steps.goes: Other behaviors are checked against the golden set before shipping.

takeaway: Try prompting and RAG first; reach for fine-tuning only for a well-defined, recurring behavior gap, and only with enough quality examples to avoid overfitting.
